2026 MLB playoff bracket, schedule, scores: Guardians vs. Rays ALCS resumes Saturday after rainout
The Brewers now await the winner of the Rays vs. Guardians ALCS before the Fall Classic gets underway
By
Kate Feldman
Oct 17, 2026
at
1:05 pm ET
2 min read
Add CBS Sports on Google
Adam Eargle, CBS Sports Design
The 2026 ALCS is set to resume Saturday night after a rainout on Friday. The Cleveland Guardians will host the Tampa Bay Rays in ALCS Game 4 at Progressive Field, with the home team looking to take a 3-1 series lead. It will be a chilly night in Northeast Ohio, with temperatures dropping into the 40s during the game, but the forecast is free of rain during the game.
There will be no more off days in the ALCS, with a potential Game 7 set for Tuesday. Whoever wins the series will be moving on to face the Milwaukee Brewers in the 2026 World Series.
The Brewers are headed to the World Series for the first time since 1982 after completing an NLCS sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night. The Brewers have secured their first National League pennant and will now attempt to win the franchise's first title. World Series Game 1 is set for Friday, Oct. 23.
The MLB playoff bracket is down to three teams. The Padres, Yankees, Braves and White Sox were all knocked out in the LDS round, while the Phillies, Astros, Red Sox and Cubs were sent packing in the Wild Card Series.
Below is a look at the full 2026  MLB playoff bracket and the playoff schedule.

The Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries will square off in the 2026 WNBA Finals -- with a slightly different schedule. The Dream will host Games 3 and 4 at State Farm Arena and Game 3 was moved up one day to Oct. 21 to accommodate the Finals game. The 2026 WNBA Finals tip off this weekend in San Francisco as the Valkyries host Game 1 at Chase Center.
The Dream and Valkyries both completed semifinal sweeps on Friday night. Atlanta knocked out the New York Liberty, while Golden State ousted the reigning champion Las Vegas Aces. The 2026 WNBA Finals are set to begin on Oct. 17.
Neither the Dream nor the Valkyries has ever won a WNBA championship. It's Atlanta's first Finals appearance since 2013. It's the first for the Valkyries, who are just in their second season as a franchise after debuting as an expansion team in 2025.
The Dream knocked the Washington Mystics out in the first round and are a perfect 5-0 in the playoffs. The Valkyries defeated the Dallas Wings in the first round, needing all three games to do so. The Finals, for the second season ever, are a best-of-seven series in 2026.
The 2026 WNBA season has been groundbreaking, on and off the court. It launched on the heels of a contentious and extended labor battle that resulted in a historic raise for the players (the salary cap increased from $1.5 million in 2025 to $7 million in 2026), and in return, the players raised the bar on a weekly basis. Multiple regular-season records fell this year, from Clark becoming the first player in WNBA history with a 40-point, 10-assist game, to Angel Reese breaking the single-game rebounding record with 26 to Kelsey Mitchell passing A'ja Wilson's single-season points record.

The ongoing theme of the 2027 NBA Draft is how wide open it will be. Amidst the backdrop of college basketball's NIL market, the upcoming draft, particularly at the top, is more unpredictable than previous years. With eight months still to go, nothing is a sure thing, a drastic shift from what we experienced in last year's cycle.
That includes the draft order itself. The 2027 NBA Draft will mark the first year of the league's lottery reform, or what is called the "3-2-1" lottery system. The new system is designed to discourage tanking.
There will now be 16 teams in the lottery (up from 14): the 10 teams that miss the postseason entirely, the No. 9 and 10 seeds in both conferences, and the losers of the No. 7 vs. No. 8 Play-In Tournament games.
There will be a new distribution of lottery balls. The teams with the three worst records would fall into the so-called "relegation" zone. They would receive only two lottery balls each. The seven remaining teams that miss the postseason entirely would receive three balls. The No. 9 and No. 10 seeds would receive two balls, and the loser of the No. 7 vs. No. 8 game would get one ball each. In total, this means there would be 37 lottery balls assigned to 16 teams.
Because that new system makes it much more difficult, if not impossible, to forecast the order, this first mock is reverse-engineered based on Tankathon's predictive win totals and is thus more based on the players than on team needs.

The home team has won the last five games in the rivalry known as the Third Saturday in October. No. 14 Tennessee spent the week sorting out its quarterback situation — George MacIntyre will start in place of the injured freshman Faizon Brandon.
Elsewhere in the SEC, Austin Simmons returns to No. 9 Ole Miss, where he opened last season as the starter before an ankle injury opened the door for Trinidad Chambliss. Now, Simmons brings No. 13 Missouri to Oxford for a gigantic showdown.
Then comes Provo at night, as No. 8 BYU hosts No. 2 Notre Dame in one of the biggest games in Cougars history. The Irish have won 16 straight games by double digits but enter Saturday with seven consecutive road losses against AP Top 10 teams. BYU hasn't beaten a top-two team since Ty Detmer stunned Miami in 1990.
Plenty can change in one week. Remember, Texas was No. 1 last week, and Florida was in the top 10 two weeks ago. Nothing is safe in college football.
Here's how our experts see the big weekend unfolding.
Michigan vs. Penn State
3:30 p.m. on CBS  CBSSports.com,  CBS Sports App  Paramount+ Premium: There is a "stoppable force vs. movable object" situation happening here with the Michigan offense against the Penn State defense, but I'm banking on the home team dictating the tempo here in a classic Big Ten rock fight. Michigan games have finished with fewer than 40 total points four times in five games -- with the lone exception being against lowly UTEP -- and even against a leaky Nittany Lions defense, it's hard to see this Michigan offense being overly explosive. On the other side, the Wolverines are still stout as ever on defense, and this seems destined to be a tense, one-score game late, with both teams struggling to top 20 points.  Pick: Under 42.5 -- Robby Kalland
No. 6 Alabama vs. No. 14 Tennessee
3:30 p.m. on ABC,  Fubo (try free): Tennessee's defense and run game have carried it to a 5-1 start. Replicating that formula against Alabama won't be possible unless the Crimson Tide shoot themselves in the foot with turnovers and special team miscues. Because the Crimson Tide won't respect the Volunteers' passing game, they'll be able to load the box and frustrate Tennessee's ground game, much like Texas did in Week 4. Offensively, Alabama has too much firepower to be fully restrained for four quarters. Look for Bama to pull away in the fourth quarter. Pick: Alabama -8.5 -- David Cobb

The WNBA will have a first-time champion in 2026. The Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream are squaring off in the 2026 WNBA Finals, and neither franchise has ever won a title. The Valkyries are in just their second season after debuting as an expansion team in 2025. The Dream, meanwhile, have been to the WNBA Finals on three occasions (2010, 2011 and 2013) but have been swept each time.
They both knocked out more-experienced teams to get here. The Valkyries took down the reigning champion Aces in the semis, while the Dream ousted the Liberty.
So who will win a historic title in 2026? Before Game 1 on Saturday, our experts are making their predictions.

Lindsay Gibbs
Jack Maloney

Dream
Valkyries
Expert explanations
Gibbs: Dream in 7. The Golden State Valkyries won the regular-season series over the Atlanta Dream 3-0, but that record doesn't quite tell the whole story. Two of those games were decided in the final minute, and all three of those meetings came in a 10-day span early in the season, with the Valkyries getting wins over the Dream on June 24, June 26 and July 4.
Those three losses were part of a five-game losing skid by the Dream, who sat at 12-9 on July 5.
The Dream have only lost five games total since, finishing the regular season with an 18-5 run. Including the postseason, Atlanta has won 10 in a row and 14 of its last 15. In August and September, the Dream led the league in offense with a 115.2 rating and were second only to the Valkyries with a 100.8 defensive rating, both about five-point improvements on their early-season ratings. Simply put, this is a different Dream team than the one the Valkyries swept this summer.
I can truly talk myself into either team winning this series – both are obviously in exceptional form and have been for the past three months, both feel like teams of destiny, both are trying to win the first title for their franchise and both are physical, dogged competitors who aren't afraid of winning ugly, which is a requirement for every title team.
The Valkyries are healthier and deeper than the Dream – the Allisha Gray injury is a big worry for Atlanta – and have home-court advantage. Defense wins championships, and the Valkyries have been far and away the best defense all season. And yet, I'm giving the Dream the edge. They have two players who have won WNBA titles in DeWanna Bonner and Jordin Canada, the far more potent offense and, while the Valkyries have the best defense, the Dream have the edge on the boards and in the paint.
In the spirit of Angel Reese and Joe Lacob, I am manifesting an epic seven-game series full of twists and turns. And, at the end, it will be a big defensive play by Reese that will seal the title for the Dream on the road in front of a raucous Ballhalla crowd on Halloween night.
From stunning Angel Reese trade to expansion ingenuity: How Dream, Valkyries broke the mold to reach Finals
Jack Maloney
Maloney: Valkyries in 6. I wish that we had more clarity on Allisha Gray's injury, what procedure she had done and what she'll be able to give the Dream -- if she's even able to play at all. Both teams have similar styles and it's difficult to get a good feel on this matchup in the best of circumstances. The uncertainty surrounding Gray makes it nearly impossible.
It is safe to assume Gray will not be close to 100% if she does play, however, especially early in the series, and that's one of the reasons I'm going with the Valkyries. Gray led the Dream in scoring during the regular season at 19 points per game, which was good for ninth in the league, and was their go-to option late in games. Jordin Canada, DeWanna Bonner and Isobel Borlase were able to make up for Gray's production in the semifinals, but I'm not super confident they can continue to hit such incredible heights, especially against the best defense in the league.
I'm going to crib here from an article I wrote about Gray's injury, which shows how incredible that trio was last round:
Canada had three of the five-highest playoff scoring performances of her career against the Liberty, and averaged 22.3 points on 62.2/61.5/100 shooting splits -- up from 11.6 points on 43.1/29.2/78.2 shooting in the regular season.
Bonner went for 15.3 points and 8.3 rebounds on 50/46.7/80 shooting splits, up from 10.4 points and six rebounds on 40.2/27.9/84.3 shooting between the Phoenix Mercury and Dream in the regular season.
And Borlase, who only had six double-digit scoring games in the regular season, came off the bench to chip in 11 points in Game 2 and 10 points in Game 3 while shooting 9 of 15, including 3 of 6 from 3-point range.
Of course, the counterpoint there is they may not have to be that good if Gray is back and Rhyne Howard doesn't shoot 31.1% from the field like she did against the Liberty. Regardless, I worry about the Dream's ability to generate consistent offense, especially with how reliant they are on forcing turnovers, and how good the Valkyries are at taking care of the ball. College football player dies: Southern Nazarene's Tyler Ulrich, 21, was injured in game last week
The Southern Nazarene safety died this week after suffering a traumatic injury during last weekend's game against Ouachita Baptist
By
Brad Crawford
Oct 17, 2026
at
10:54 am ET
1 min read
Add CBS Sports on Google
Getty Images
Southern Nazarene University safety Tyler Ulrich died this week after suffering a traumatic injury during a game on Oct. 10 at Ouachita Baptist University, the university announced.
A sophomore at the Division II private school in Bethany, Oklahoma, the 21-year-old Ulrich was hospitalized for five days prior to his passing. Saturday's game against Southwestern Oklahoma State University has been canceled.
Last week's matchup with Ouachita Baptist in Arkadelphia, Arkansas, was delayed for nearly an hour while Ulrich reportedly received medical attention on the field before being transported to a hospital.
Ulrich was one of Southern Nazarene's top defensive players, ranking third on the team with 36 tackles.
Southern Nazarene University president Keith Newman said in a statement Thursday that since Ulrich was hospitalized, he was "continually surrounded by the love, prayers, and presence of his family, teammates, and dear friends."
"Please keep Tyler's family, teammates, coaches, and friends in your continued prayers during this unimaginably difficult time," Newman said.
"It is with heavy hearts that we share the loss of our SNU football player, Tyler Ulrich,"  SNU Athletics said in a post on its X account. "This loss is deeply felt across our campus. Our hearts are with his family, friends, teammates, and everyone who knew him. We ask that you join us in lifting them up in prayer."
Southern Nazarene coach Dustin Hada  posted a tribute on his X account, saying Tyler was a "Man of God, ultimate example of quiet strength, loyal, worker, joyous. That's who Tyler was!!"
Southern Nazarene wrote in a Facebook post Thursday the school is grieving.
"This loss is deeply felt across our campus. Our hearts are with his family, friends, teammates, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him. We ask that you join us in lifting them up in prayer during this incredibly difficult time," the statement reads.
During an interview with KOCO News ABC 5, Ulrich's prep football coach Azle High School in Azle, Texas, raved about his former player's character.
"Tyler is built. He is. He looks like a professional football player to me," Jason Vines said. "When I think of good, I think of Tyler Ulrich. One of the sweetest young men I've ever been around, and ever known."
A GoFundMe has been created to assist the Ulrich family during this time of loss.
